heuristics: H1: the class walk on H/mu6 (H the 2^20-th powers in Z_r^*, multiplicative steps with 64 multipliers in H) behaves as a random mapping on M = (r-1)/(6*2^20) classes; S = ceil(2 sqrt(13/20 M)) points give a tame-wild collision with probability 1 - exp(-S^2/(4M)) = 0.477954.

H2: the walk advances 256 records in rounds, so detection of a merged pair costs at most 256 times the merged path's first-distinguished-point delay (mean 2^90 per trail); the procedure's budget of S + 2^108 points loses at most 2 e^-1024 this way. Cap truncation of merged paths loses at most 2^-9; in-trail cycles at most 1.2e-5; a bounded distinguished-point table with 256-slot buckets overflows with probability at most 2^-52. All are stated in proof.md section 4.

H3: the non-addition work of a walk point is measured by Callgrind (1895.45 instructions per point, 512 points over 256 records, production tables); the DP store, restart and table-build costs are measured or bounded analytically as stated in proof.md section 5.
limitations: H1 is an unproved heuristic; the fresh toy runs (4000 trials on 32- and 36-bit prime-order toy groups with the mu6 action) support it at the claim budget, but nothing is tested at production size.
The claimed success 0.40 is below the Wilson 95% lower bound 0.4227 of the fresh toy runs, minus the stated losses (total 0.00196).

The walk's additions are charged as batched affine reference units; the measured kernel performs unbatched affine additions, each with its own inversion, so the batched price is a convention, not a measured batched implementation.
The kernel reuses 16 precomputed restart exponents and charges fresh sampling as a bound; the table-build normalisation and other sampling, Tonelli-Shanks and DP work are analytic bounds.
Peak memory is about 19.4 GB, dominated by the bounded distinguished-point table.
Analytic production cost; no production-size execution. Not a practical attack.
